fetched_contents.text: Serological Detection of Varicella-Zoster Virus-Specific Immunoglobulin G by an Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay Using Glycoprotein Antigen Abstract Since the introduction of varicella vaccination in several countries, there has been an urgent need for commercially available test procedures that allow highly sensitive and specific quantitative determination of the varicella-zoster virus (VZV)-specific immune status, including immunity postimmunization. This study compared the performance of two enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays (ELISAs) for the sensitive and specific determination of VZV-specific immunoglobulin G (IgG) in seronegative and latently infected persons, as well as in vaccinees. One ELISA is based on the detection of antibody to VZV-specific envelope glycoproteins (gp), and the other comprises the whole antigen extract prepared from VZV-infected cells. A modified standard fluorescent-antibody-to-membrane-antigen (FAMA) assay was used as a reference. An excellent sensitivity (100%) in relation to FAMA was demonstrated for the gpELISA (Virion\Serion), while the non-gpELISA (Dade Behring) had a lower sensitivity (83%) when sera from latently infected persons were tested. After postvaccinal immunity was measured, a sensitivity of 87% was achieved with gpELISA, whereas the ELISA incorporating antigen extract of VZV-infected cells had a sensitivity of 78%. Excellent specificity (100%) was calculated for both the gpELISA and the non-gpELISA. In conclusion, SERION ELISA classic VZV IgG is useful for the sensitive and specific quantitative determination of VZV immune status after natural infection. The test can also be recommended for measuring antibody response after varicella vaccination, particularly after the cutoff value was optimized. ---------------------------------------- The determination of specific immunoglobulin G (IgG) is of great significance for obtaining serological proof of immunity to varicella-zoster virus (VZV) since patient histories cannot be regarded as reliable indicators of past primary infections (9). In particular, laboratory determination of the status of immunity to VZV has been recommended (i) in immunocompromised patients after exposure to VZV and prior to varicella vaccination (11), (ii) in pregnant women or those considering pregnancy with a history of exposure to VZV or an uncertain history with regard to varicella (19), and (iii) in health workers prior to varicella vaccination or after exposure to VZV (3). After the introduction of universal varicella vaccination in a number of countries, such as in Germany (14), the indications for measuring VZV-specific IgG antibodies have been broadened. In particular, a postimmunization serological testing of immunity has been required for immunocompromised vaccinees and health workers (18). In addition, quantitative monitoring of changes in VZV antibody levels in a population is a component of varicella vaccination surveillance (10). In most diagnostic laboratories, the methodological opportunities for testing immunity after varicella vaccination are fairly limited. The main reason for that is the low sensitivity of the currently available commercial laboratory assays, in particular of different modifications of the enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) (6). A general consensus is that the most reliable assay for determining the status of immunity to VZV is the fluorescent-antibody-to-membrane-antigen (FAMA) test detecting antibodies specific to the viral envelope glycoproteins (gp) (4, 7). Thus, these antibodies can reflect the specific cellular immunity that plays the key role in protection against VZV infections (5). However, the time-consuming procedure for measuring cellular immunity precludes its routine use (22). To date, the FAMA procedure can only be performed as a modified in-house test that is labor-intensive and requires considerable experience in handling VZV, and interpretation of the test results is subjective. Since there is no sufficient experience in storage of FAMA, the results can only be obtained within several days. Furthermore, the use of diploid fibroblasts derived from different human origins generally prevents attempts to achieve standardization and automation. Practical experience with the FAMA kit commercially produced by Viran Clinical Diagnostics (Stevensville, MI) suggested that the results are not reproducible (1). Finally, Merck Research Laboratories (West Point, PA) developed VZV gp-specific ELISA (21), but this assay is not available commercially. fetched_contents.text: Current Methods for the Detection of Antibodies of Varicella-Zoster Virus: A Review Abstract Infection with the varicella-zoster virus (VZV) causes chickenpox and shingles, which lead to significant morbidity and mortality globally. The detection of serum VZV-specific antibodies is important for the clinical diagnosis and sero-epidemiological research of VZV infection, and for assessing the effect of VZV vaccine immunization. Over recent decades, a variety of methods for VZV antibody detection have been developed. This review summarizes and compares the current methods for detecting VZV antibodies, and discussed future directions for this field. Keywords: varicella-zoster virus (VZV), antibody detection methods, FAMA, ELISA 1. Introduction Varicella-zoster virus (VZV) is a highly contagious alpha-herpesvirus that infects more than 90% of people worldwide [1,2]. Chickenpox (varicella) is the outcome of primary infection with VZV and mainly affects children. As per the report published by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 2014, the minimum of the annual global disease burden of chickenpox was estimated to be 140 million cases, of which 4.2 million have severe complications leading to hospitalization and death [3]. Although usually a mild and self-limiting illness, chickenpox poses a greater risk of severe disease to pregnant women, neonates, VZV-seronegative adults, and immunocompromised individuals [4]. The reactivation of latent VZV causes shingles (herpes zoster), which occurs mainly in people ≥50 years of age and is usually associated with intense neuralgia [5]. It was estimated that about one third of individuals who have had chickenpox will develop shingles [6]. The incidence and severity of shingles increases with age or immunosuppression [7]. Recent studies have shown that COVID-19 vaccination may also increase the risk of VZV reactivation and thus potentially increase the incidence of shingles, especially in the elderly population [8,9,10]. To date, there is still no specific cure for VZV-induced diseases. Vaccination is among the most cost-effective ways for preventing chickenpox and shingles. The most widely used chickenpox vaccines consist of the Oka strain of live-attenuated VZV (vOka), and there are currently two kinds of shingles vaccines on the market, including a live-attenuated vaccine also based on vOka (ZOSTAVAX®, Merck Sharp & Dohme, Rahway, NJ, USA) and a recombinant subunit vaccine based on VZV glycoprotein E (Shingrix®, GlaxoSmithKline, Brentford, Middlesex, UK) [6,11,12]. However, the use of these vaccines is not universal and thus a large proportion of the global population has not been vaccinated against VZV. Consequently, VZV infection is still prevalent and accounts for a significant disease burden worldwide. Laboratory testing is essential for the diagnosis and surveillance of VZV-induced diseases. Virus isolation was once the “gold standard” for the diagnosis of VZV infection [13,14]. However, this method is time-consuming and not readily accessible, and has thus been replaced by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for the detection of viral DNA and direct fluorescence assays (DFA) for the detection of viral proteins [15,16]. Most recently, a recombinase-aided amplification-lateral flow system (RAA-LF) has been used for the rapid detection of VZV DNA, which is easier to use and requires no equipment [17]. PCR is currently regarded as the most sensitive and reliable method for VZV detection [14]. Meanwhile, serological assays, which detect VZV-specific antibodies, also represent reliable diagnostic tools in the detection of VZV infection, and have been implemented as complementary approaches to PCR. Furthermore, since the quantitative detection of anti-VZV antibody is necessary for measuring the infection history and evaluating the immune status against VZV in the population, serological assays have been widely used in epidemiological investigations of VZV and evaluations of immune responses to VZV vaccination. These assays include the fluorescent-antibody-to-membrane-antigen (FAMA) test, the complement fixation (CF) test, the immune adherence hemagglutination assay (IAHA), the latex agglutination (LA) test, the radioimmunoassay (RIA), the neutralization assay, the chemiluminescent immunoassay (CLIA), the enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), the immunofluorescence assay (IFA), the time-resolved fluorescence immunoassay (TRFIA), and the lateral flow immunochromatographic assay (LFIA). Among these tests, FAMA and ELISA are the most widely used. On the other hand, the CF test has low sensitivity, while RIA uses harmful radioactive materials; therefore, neither method has been widely used in recent years. Herein, we review the existing serological assays for the detection of anti-VZV antibodies and compare their advantages and limitations. This paper could help clinicians and technicians to choose the appropriate serological method for diagnosing VZV infection or assessing the efficacy of VZV vaccines. 2. fetched_contents.text: Validity of medical record documented varicella-zoster virus among unvaccinated cohorts Abstract Background: A varicella diagnosis or verification of disease history by any healthcare provider is currently accepted for determining evidence of immunity by the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP). Healthcare workers' recall of prior varicella infection or vaccination is only moderately reliable as a proxy for actual serostatus, and the evidence suggests that recall accuracy varies by age, vaccination history, and whether the recall is self-reported versus documented. The strongest direct evidence comes from studies of varicella history among unvaccinated cohorts, which show that parent/patient recall is imperfect, while medical record documentation is more accurate in some settings.

First, the proportion of workers who correctly recall varicella status is not uniformly high. In a study of unvaccinated children aged 5–19 years, parent/patient recall of varicella history increased with age from 60% for 5–9-year-olds to 91% for 15–19-year-olds, but this still leaves substantial room for error [N2-F3]. This pattern implies that recall accuracy is not perfect, even among older children and adolescents, and therefore cannot be assumed to be high in healthcare workers without direct comparison. The same study also reports that the specificity of “any MR documentation” and “sick visit documentation” was much higher than parent/patient recall in most age groups, though the differences were statistically significant only for 10–14-year-olds comparing sick visit documentation to parent/patient recall [N2-F3]. This directly supports the conclusion that recall alone is not a reliable substitute for documentation.

Second, false positives and false negatives are identified in recall studies. The study notes that medical record documentation of a sick visit for varicella had a positive predictive value of 96% for the youngest group, 92% for the middle group, and 99% for the oldest group, while parent/patient recall had lower predictive value [N2-F3]. This means that recall can falsely suggest immunity when there is none, and that it is also less able to detect true immunity. The cited source also says that parent/patient recall was compared with MR documentation as a predictor of VZV immunity, and that the authors concluded that sick-visit documentation was an accurate predictor of seropositivity [N2-F3]. This framing reinforces that recall can miss true immunity and can also falsely label people as immune.

Third, factors associated with recall error include vaccination history and age. The evidence here is mixed but clear in direction: older age is associated with better recall, whereas younger age is associated with worse recall [N2-F3]. The same study also implies that vaccination history matters because it is one of the sources of varicella history being recalled [N2-F3]. The broader recall literature in healthcare workers further suggests that self-reported vaccination histories can be unreliable: a systematic review found that recall and home-based records provide relatively concordant vaccination histories in some settings, but both have poor agreement with facility-based records and serology [N3-R1]. Another study found that healthcare workers who received vaccine for only some of the preceding five seasons were more likely to have ≥2 errors in their recall than those vaccinated all five seasons [N3-R2][N3-R3]. This supports the conclusion that vaccination history is not a guarantee of accurate recall and that partial or inconsistent vaccination histories increase recall error.

A separate study on varicella seroprevalence among healthcare workers also shows that recall bias is relevant to serostatus interpretation. It reports that HCW seroprevalence was 91.2% in healthcare workers and 92.1% in students, and that the sensitivity, specificity, positive, and negative values were reported [N2-R3]. While this item does not provide a full table of performance metrics, it is consistent with the idea that recall-based classification of serostatus is imperfect because it must be validated against laboratory results. The broader literature on self-reported medical history also emphasizes that recall error can alter conclusions about relationships among socioeconomic, clinical, and other variables [N4-R5]. This is important because recall-based determination of VZV serostatus can create systematic bias if workers falsely report immunity or lack of immunity.

In summary, healthcare workers’ recall aligns poorly with actual serostatus in the evidence provided. The proportion who correctly recall varicella status is not consistently high, false positives and false negatives are present, and recall error is associated with younger age and inconsistent vaccination history [N2-F3][N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R3]. Recall is therefore only a weak proxy for true serostatus and should not be relied on alone [N2-F3][N4-R5].

The diagnostic performance evidence for VZV serostatus is dominated by assays and reference standards that emphasize sensitivity, specificity, and validation against a gold standard, with performance varying by population and setting. The most commonly used assays are enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays (ELISAs), fluorescent-antibody-to-membrane-antigen (FAMA) assays, and newer rapid or lateral-flow immunochromatographic assays (LFIA/LFAs). The reference standards used in the evidence include sera from seronegative and latently infected persons, vaccinees, and modified FAMA assays.

First, the assays commonly used for VZV serostatus include ELISA and FAMA. A 2012 study evaluated three commercial VZV IgG ELISAs and reported sensitivities of 99.6% and 99.2% for two of them, while specificity was excellent but not fully specified in the excerpt [N1-R5]. Another review notes that FAMA is considered the “gold standard” for VZV antibody detection because it detects antibodies specific to viral proteins on infected cells and is widely used in research [N1-F2]. A later study compared two ELISAs for VZV-specific IgG and found excellent sensitivity and specificity for the gpELISA and excellent specificity for the non-gpELISA, though the gpELISA had lower sensitivity in some contexts [N1-F1]. A 2023 review also highlights that rapid, sensitive, and specific lateral-flow immunochromatographic assays are being developed for prior VZV infection or varicella/zoster vaccination [N1-R4]. Taken together, the evidence shows that ELISA and FAMA remain the mainstay, while LFIA/LFAs are emerging as faster alternatives.

Second, reported sensitivity and specificity values across studies are generally very high, but not universally identical. The review evidence states that the SERION ELISA classic VZV IgG had the highest sensitivity (99.6%) and specificity (100%) in one study [N1-R3]. In another study, the Enzygnost anti-VZV/IgG and the Serion ELISA Classic VZV IgG showed sensitivities of 99.6% and 99.2%, respectively, while the Euroimmun anti-VZV/IgG had a lower sensitivity [N1-R5]. The review also notes that FAMA is the most extensively validated assay and is considered the “gold standard” [N1-F2]. In contrast, the study on ELISAs in seronegative and latently infected persons found that one ELISA had 100% sensitivity relative to FAMA, while the other had lower sensitivity for latently infected persons [N1-F1]. These differences show that test performance depends on the assay design and the population being tested.

Third, test performance changes by population and setting. The review emphasizes that FAMA is preferred for determining immunity after natural infection because it reflects cellular immunity and protection against VZV infection [N1-F2]. It also notes that ELISA has been used in most diagnostic laboratories, but that current commercial assays have limited sensitivity, especially compared to FAMA [N1-F2]. The same source states that postimmunization serological testing is required for immunocompromised vaccinees and health workers, and that quantitative monitoring of antibody levels is important for vaccination surveillance [N1-F2]. This indicates that reliability is highest in settings where FAMA is available or where ELISAs have been optimized for postvaccination immunity [N1-F1][N1-F2]. In contrast, the evidence suggests that rapid assays can be sensitive and specific but are still being developed [N1-R4].

Overall, the diagnostic performance evidence supports a strong conclusion: VZV serostatus is commonly assessed with ELISA and FAMA, with reported sensitivities often near 99% and specificity also excellent [N1-R3][N1-R5][N1-F1][N1-F2]. However, performance is not uniform across assays and populations; some ELISAs have lower sensitivity for latently infected persons, and FAMA remains the most validated reference standard [N1-F1][N1-F2]. This means reliability is highest when assays are validated against FAMA or in settings where postimmunization immunity is well-characterized [N1-F1][N1-F2].

Second, recall accuracy trends across age, vaccination, and other covariates show that recall is generally worse in younger individuals and can be influenced by vaccination history. Recall bias differs from medical record documentation in that documented histories are more reliable, with sick-visit documentation showing higher specificity than parent/patient recall in some settings [N2-F3]. Therefore, recall alone is not a reliable proxy for true serostatus in healthcare workers.

Recall is not generally a reliable substitute for direct serostatus testing, especially when the goal is to determine whether someone has true VZV immunity or is seronegative. The evidence supports that recall is acceptable only under limited conditions, misleading otherwise, and subject to meaningful limitations as a proxy for true serostatus.

First, recall is acceptable only when the consequences of false positives or false negatives are low, and when documentation or other corroborating evidence is available. The evidence on self-reported medical history shows that recall can have fair-to-excellent test-retest reliability for some questions, but this does not mean it is reliable for all health-related recall tasks [N4-R1]. It also notes that the validity of self-reported data depends on respondents’ ability to report accurately, eliminate recall bias, and ensure consistency [N4-R2]. In the context of VZV serostatus, recall is therefore acceptable only when used cautiously, paired with documentation, or when the clinical or epidemiological risk of misclassification is minimal [N4-R2][N4-R5]. The opposite is true for healthcare workers’ recall of varicella history: the study of unvaccinated children showed that medical record documentation was more accurate than parent/patient recall, and that recall was especially less accurate in younger children [N2-F3]. This directly supports the idea that recall is misleading when it is the only basis for serostatus determination.

Second, recall error can affect clinical decisions and outbreak control. The evidence shows that recall-based determination of serostatus can create systematic bias. The broader self-report literature states that recall error can alter conclusions about relationships among socioeconomic, clinical, and other variables [N4-R5]. In outbreak control settings, this is particularly dangerous because false positives may lead to unnecessary vaccination or restriction of workers who are actually immune, while false negatives may allow infected workers to remain in settings where they can spread VZV. The same evidence on varicella history among unvaccinated cohorts shows that parent/patient recall was compared with MR documentation as a predictor of VZV immunity, and that sick-visit documentation was an accurate predictor of seropositivity [N2-F3]. This means that recall can misclassify workers and therefore affect decisions about immunity documentation, vaccination, and workplace safety.

Third, the limitations of self-report as a proxy for true serostatus are clear. Recall is vulnerable to age-related recall bias, vaccination history inconsistencies, and recall failure. In the healthcare worker recall literature, a systematic review found that recall and home-based records provide relatively concordant vaccination histories in some settings, but both have poor agreement with facility-based records and serology [N3-R1]. Another study found that healthcare workers who received vaccine for only some of the preceding five seasons were more likely to have ≥2 errors in their recall than those vaccinated all five seasons [N3-R2][N3-R3]. In the VZV-specific evidence, the study of unvaccinated children aged 5–19 years found that parent/patient recall improved with age but was still imperfect, and that medical record documentation had higher specificity than parent/patient recall [N2-F3]. These findings together show that self-report is not a robust proxy for true serostatus and can systematically underestimate or overestimate immunity.

Overall, the general validity of using recall instead of direct serostatus testing is weak. Recall is acceptable only in limited settings where documentation or other validation is available and the stakes of misclassification are low [N4-R1][N4-R2]. It is misleading when used as the sole basis for serostatus determination, especially in healthcare workers, because recall can miss true immunity or falsely suggest immunity, and because recall error is associated with age and inconsistent vaccination history [N2-F3][N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R3]. As a proxy for true serostatus, recall is therefore best treated as a weak and context-dependent cue rather than a substitute for direct testing [N4-R5][N2-F3].

Healthcare workers’ recall of prior varicella infection or vaccination is only **moderately reliable** as a proxy for actual serostatus. - the consequences of false positives or false negatives are low,  
- documentation or other corroborating evidence is available, and  
- the clinical or epidemiological risk of misclassification is minimal [N4-R2][N9].

Based on the available evidence, healthcare workers’ recall of their personal medical history is **not sufficiently reliable** to accurately determine VZV serostatus on its own. Recall is useful in some limited settings, but it is generally **not a substitute for direct serostatus testing** when the goal is to determine whether someone has true immunity or is seronegative [N4-R2][N9]. The reliability of recall depends heavily on the context, and it is particularly weak when used as the sole basis for serostatus determination [N9].

### 1. Diagnostic performance metrics for VZV serostatus: what assays and standards are used?

The diagnostic performance evidence is dominated by assays and reference standards that emphasize **sensitivity, specificity, and validation against a gold standard**. The most commonly used assays are **enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays (ELISAs)** and the **fluorescent-antibody-to-membrane-antigen (FAMA) assay**, with newer rapid or lateral-flow immunochromatographic assays also being developed [N1-F2][N1-R4]. The reference standards used in the evidence include sera from **seronegative and latently infected persons, vaccinees, and modified FAMA assays** [N1-F1][N1-F2].

Reported sensitivity and specificity values across studies are generally very high, but not identical across assays or populations. For example, one study reported sensitivities of **99.6% and 99.2%** for two commercial ELISAs, while another found **excellent sensitivity and specificity** for the gpELISA and excellent specificity for the non-gpELISA [N1-R5][N1-F1]. A 2023 review also highlights that **rapid, sensitive, and specific lateral-flow immunochromatographic assays** are being developed for prior VZV infection or varicella/zoster vaccination [N1-R4]. Healthcare workers’ recall of prior varicella infection or vaccination is only **moderately reliable** as a proxy for actual serostatus. The same unvaccinated children study found that **medical record documentation had higher specificity than parent/patient recall** in most age groups [N2-F3]. It also reports that parent/patient recall was compared with MR documentation as a predictor of VZV immunity, and that the authors concluded that sick-visit documentation was an accurate predictor of seropositivity [N2-F3]. In the broader healthcare worker recall literature, a systematic review found that recall and home-based records provide relatively concordant vaccination histories in some settings, but both have poor agreement with facility-based records and serology [N3-R1]. Another study found that healthcare workers who received vaccine for only some of the preceding five seasons were more likely to have **≥2 errors in their recall** than those vaccinated all five seasons [N3-R2][N3-R3]. This shows that recall error is not limited to age; it is also linked to partial or inconsistent vaccination histories.

Recall is **acceptable only under limited conditions**, and it is **misleading otherwise**. The evidence supports that recall is acceptable when:

- the consequences of false positives or false negatives are low,  
- documentation or other corroborating evidence is available, and  
- the clinical or epidemiological risk of misclassification is minimal [N4-R2][N9].
